A special MP-MLA court has allowed the prosecution to withdraw a case against 25 BJP leaders and Hindu activists, including Uttar Pradesh Minister Kapil Dev Agarwal, former Union Minister Sanjeev Balyan and former State Minister Suresh Rana, in connection with a 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots-related case.
Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate/MP-MLA court judge Devendra Kumar Faujdar allowed the prosecution's application seeking withdrawal of the case on Wednesday, prosecution officer Rahul Singh said.
The accused were facing trial for allegedly violating prohibitory orders, obstructing public servants in the discharge of their duties, and inciting communal tension through speeches at a mahapanchayat held at Nagla Mador in the district on July 31, 2013, Mr. Singh told PTI on Thursday (August 13, 2026).
The accused included Mr. Agarwal, Mr. Balyan, Mr. Rana, former Uttar Pradesh Minister Ashok Kataria, former BJP MPs Bhartendu Singh and Sohanvir Singh, former BJP MLAs Ashok Kansal and Umesh Malik, VHP leader Sadhvi Prachi and Narsinghanand of Dasna Shiv Temple, among others.
The prosecution moved the application following the Uttar Pradesh government's decision to withdraw the case, Mr. Singh said.
The 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots and subsequent violence in neighbouring districts left more than 60 people dead and displaced over 40,000, according to official figures.

Assam CM Himanta Sarma calls for peace as fresh clash erupts along border with Arunachal Pradesh
Fresh clashes erupted between protestors from Assam and Arunachal Pradesh in Dhemaji district amid the ongoing call for an economic blockade of Itanagar.
Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma has called for peace after reports of clashes along the border with Arunachal Pradesh emerged on Thursday.
Fresh clashes erupted between protestors from Assam and Arunachal Pradesh in Dhemaji district, reported news agency PTI.
The escalation prompted Arunachal police to fire into the air to control the mob as the protest over an indefinite economic blockade against the Himalayan state entered its second day.
"When the blockade was going on, some people from Arunachal Pradesh indulged in stone pelting on protesters from Assam, and some persons sustained minor injuries. This led to a scuffle between the two sides," an official told news agency PTI.
Assam CM urges for ‘peace and harmony’
Addressing the clashes, chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma urged for peace and calm.
"I appeal to the people of Assam and Arunachal to maintain peace and harmony. Boundaries may define our States, but they can never divide our hearts," he wrote on X.
Along with the chief minister, MPs from Assam and Arunachal Pradesh also called for peace and calm in the region.
“We must live together harmoniously as brothers and sisters and settle any land dispute through peaceful negotiation only,” said union parliamentary affairs Kiren Rijiju in a video message on X.
What led to the clash?
The Takam Mising Porin Kebang (TMPK), the apex student organisation of Assam's Mising community, launched an indefinite economic blockade against Arunachal on Wednesday against the alleged firing in which 12 indigenous people from Assam were injured over land-encroachment issues.
Along with TMPK, other local social groups like Mising Mimag Kebang (MMK) and Takam Mising Mahila Kebang (TMMK) have supported the blockade and stopped all vehicles, barring emergency and school transportation, from coming or going to Arunachal Pradesh at the entry points.
The organisations have called for an early resolution of the Assam-Arunachal Pradesh border dispute, action against the "miscreants" who had fired and an end to alleged encroachment on Assam land.
The conflict between Assam and Arunachal also dates back to 1987, when Arunachal attained full statehood.
After Arunachal Pradesh became a state, a tripartite committee was appointed, which recommended that certain territories be transferred from Assam to Arunachal Pradesh.
In 2022, chief ministers Himanta Biswa Sarma and Pema Khandu signed the Namsai Declaration to narrow down disputes from 123 villages to a manageable subset through regional committees.
Referring to this, Sarma wrote on X: "Only 52 villages remain, and both Governments will continue discussions in the same spirit to resolve the dispute completely."
(With inputs from PTI)

Vande Mataram or the National Song will be sung from the ramparts of the Red Fort in New Delhi for the first time on Independence Day, preceding the National Anthem. It is also the 150th anniversary of the adoption of Bankim Chandra Chatterjee’s Vande Mataram as the National Song. But the original adopted version included only the first two stanzas. Recently, the Centre notified that all six stanzas would have to be sung.
The Centre issued guidelines on February 11, 2026, for the rendition of the National Song at public gatherings, schools, and official government functions, among others. This comes after the passing of the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Act, 2026, which amended the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. It is now a criminal offence to intentionally disrupt, obstruct, or prevent the singing of the Vande Mataram.
The duration of singing and specific directions for playing by a band, among other rules, have also been mentioned in the circular.
Vande Mataram to precede Jana Gana Mana
The circular mentions that the National Song Vande Mataramshall be played or sung before the National Anthem‘Jana Gana Mana’ on all occasions when both are to be played or sung.
Vande Mataram duration
The total duration of the National Song must be “approximately 3 minutes 10 seconds.”
If played by a band, it should be preceded by a “by a roll of drums to assist the audience to know that the National Song is going to be played, unless there is some other specific indication that the National Song is about to be played, as for example, when fanfares are sounded before the National Song is played.”
The circular adds that “the duration of the roll, in terms of marching drill, will be 7 paces in slow march. The roll will start slowly, ascend to as loud a volume as possible and then gradually decreases to original softness, but remaining audible until the seventh beat. One beat rest will then be observed before commencing the National Song.”
Vande Mataram: Occasions for rendition
- Civil Investitures
- On arrival of the President at formal State functions and other functions organized by the Government and on his departure from such functions
- Immediately before and after the President addresses the Nation over All India Radio and Television
- On arrival of the Governor/Lieutenant Governor at formal State functions within his State/Union Territory and on his departure from such functions
- When the National Flag is brought on parade
Rules for mass singing
The National Song shall be played accompanied by mass singing on these occasions:
- On the unfurling of the National Flag, on cultural occasions or ceremonial functions other than parades
- On the arrival of the President at any Government or Public function (but excluding formal State functions) and also immediately before his departure from such functions
- On all occasions when the National Song is sung, the official version shall be recited accompanied by mass singing
- The National Song may be sung on occasions which, although not strictly ceremonial, are nevertheless invested with significance because of the presence of Ministers etc
- In all schools, the day’s work may begin with community singing of the National Song
Standing mandatory during National Song
The circular mentions specific rules of standing when the National Song is played or sung:
- Whenever the official version of the National Song is sung or played, the audience shall stand to attention.
- However, when, in the course of a newsreel or documentary, the National Song is played as part of the film, it is not expected of the audience to stand, as standing is bound to interrupt the exhibition of the film and would create disorder and confusion rather than add to the dignity of the National Song.
Vande Mataram: All six stanzas
The directive has given the lyrics for the National Song, and it includes all six stanzas of Vande Mataram. The lyrics to be sung or played are as follows:
Vande Mataram!
Sujalam suphalam malayaja-sitalam,
Sasya-syamalam Mataram!
Vande Mataram!
Subhra-jyotsnam pulakita-yaminim,
Phulla-kusumita druma-dala-sobhinim,
Suhasinim sumadhura bhasinim,
Sukhadam varadam Mataram!
Vande Mataram!
Koti-koti kantha kalakala ninada karale,
Koti-koti bhujair dhrta kharakaravale,
Ke bole Ma tumi abale!
Bahubaladharinim namami tarinim,
Ripudala-varinim Mataram!
Vande Mataram!
Tumi vidya, tumi dharma,
Tumi hrdi, tumi marma,
Tvam hi pranah sarire!
Bahute tumi Ma sakti,
Hrdaye tumi Ma bhakti,
Tomarai pratima gadi mandire-mandire.
Vande Mataram!
Tvam hi Durga dasa-praharana-dharini,
Kamala kamala-dala-viharini,
Vani vidya-dayini,
Namami tvam namami kamalam,
Amalam atulam,
Sujalam suphalam Mataram!
Vande Mataram!
Syamalam saralam susmitam bhusitam,
Dharanim bharanim Mataram!
Vande Mataram!

A Karnataka Health Department Food Safety Division team resumed inspection of eateries and other establishments in Bengaluru on Wednesday (August 12, 2026).
The team inspected the canteen at the department’s headquarters in Bengaluru, where it seized expired food items and flagged hygiene violations.
Officials inspected hotels and other food business establishments located in the premises of Vidhana Soudha, Legislators’ Home and the MS Building in Bengaluru.
According to officials, expired food products, such as idli rava and coconut powder, were found in the kitchen of the Arogya Soudha canteen on Magadi Road. Food products were not stored in accordance with FSSAI guidelines. Pest control measures had not been carried out, leaving the premises in an unhygienic condition, officials said.
In a statement, the Food Safety and Drug Administration department said an advisory notice was issued in view of the unhygienic conditions observed at the canteen. Legal proceedings will be initiated before the Adjudicating Officer, it stated.
During inspection of a Nandini parlour located in the premises, officials found violations relating to labelling requirements, and issued an advisory notice, according to the statement.
Four hotels located in the premises of government buildings were inspected, with various deficiencies observed. Advisory notices were issued to the hotels concerned, according to the department.
Officials inspected a restaurant run by a private operator inside Legislators’ House, adjacent to Vidhana Soudha, and found unhygienic conditions. An advisory notice was issued. Among other things, cockroaches were found in the kitchen, they claimed.
A hotel located in the premises of the MS Building was inspected. The establishment was found to be unhygienic and was subsequently closed, the department stated.
The food business operator submitted an undertaking stating that the deficiencies would be rectified and that the hotel would be reopened only after obtaining permission from the Commissioner, in accordance with the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the applicable rules, it stated.
Action would be initiated against the food business operator, the department added.
Eateries told to comply with food safety rules
Food business operators have been instructed to strictly comply with the Food Safety and Standards Act and the applicable rules and regulations, the department said.
Any violation relating to food quality, safety, hygiene, proper storage, labelling or food handling practices would invite strict legal action under the law, it added.
The department has been conducting such drives as part of special food safety inspections across all zones of Bengaluru Urban District and the Greater Bengaluru Area, covering three-star and five-star hotels to verify compliance with the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the Food Safety and Standards (Licensing and Registration of Food Businesses) Regulations, 2011.
Recently, 60 three-star and five-star hotels in Bengaluru Urban District were inspected, and 77 food samples were collected and sent to food laboratories for analysis.

A patient recently came to the clinic after recovering from a viral fever. The fever had settled, the initial tests were no longer concerning and he had started going back to work. But he was still feeling unusually tired. On some days, he felt almost normal. On others, even routine activity left him exhausted. A few days later, he developed body ache and a mild fever again. His immediate concern was that the first infection had returned.
This is a situation that can be confusing for patients, particularly during the monsoon, when dengue, chikungunya, influenza, H1N1 and other infectious microbes can circulate at the same time. The symptoms can overlap and recovery is not always a straight line.
Fever is one of the most visible signs of an infection, so people often use it as a measure of recovery. Once the temperature becomes normal, they expect their energy to return as well. But the body may take longer to recover.
During an infection, a person may eat less, lose fluids, sleep poorly and remain physically inactive for several days. The immune response to the infection also takes time to settle. As a result, weakness, poor appetite, body ache and reduced stamina may continue even after the fever has gone. This does not necessarily mean that the infection is still active. A negative test is reassuring, but it is not a measure of how quickly the body has regained its strength.
One reason is that people often return to their routine too quickly. After several days of illness, a person may feel better for a day or two and resume full working hours, exercise or travel. The following day, the fatigue may become much more pronounced.
This can feel like a relapse but sometimes it is simply the result of doing more than the body is ready for. A gradual return to activity is therefore important. Strenuous exercise should not be resumed simply because the fever has disappeared.
This is where overlapping infections become important. A person recovering from one viral infection can still be exposed to another infection. Seasonal infections may produce similar early symptoms such as fever, body ache, headache and fatigue. It can, therefore, be difficult to determine from symptoms alone whether someone is still recovering or has developed another illness. Government guidance also notes that one infection does not necessarily exclude another, and co-infections can occur.
For example, a patient may recover from influenza, return to work and then develop fever again after a fresh exposure. Another person may initially be diagnosed with a viral fever and later test positive for dengue. These situations need clinical assessment rather than assuming that every recurrence of weakness is simply “post-viral fatigue.”
There is another reason why a returning patient should not simply be reassured because the fever has come down. In dengue, the period when the fever starts settling can be important. The critical phase generally occurs around this time in patients who develop complications. Warning signs include persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, bleeding, increasing drowsiness, difficulty breathing, restlessness or reduced urine output. These symptoms require prompt medical evaluation.
Platelet count is also not the only measure of recovery in dengue. Hydration, blood pressure, haematocrit (percentage of your blood that is made up of red blood cells and is evidence of plasma leakage) and the patient’s overall clinical condition are important in deciding how the illness is progressing.
If there is no evidence of a continuing or new infection, the focus is usually on recovery. Adequate sleep, regular, balanced meals, sufficient fluids and gradual physical activity are important.
It is also important not to start antibiotics simply because fatigue continues. Antibiotics do not treat viral infections. Steroids and other medicines should similarly not be taken without a clear medical reason.
Most people gradually improve. But persistent or worsening symptoms deserve reassessment. A returning fever, breathlessness, chest discomfort, repeated vomiting, fainting, confusion, reduced urine output or a significant deterioration in general health should not be dismissed as weakness after a viral infection.
The same applies when symptoms continue for longer than expected without any clear improvement. The important point is that recovery from an infection is not always linear.
(Dr Chatterjee is Senior Consultant, Internal Medicine, Indraprastha Apollo Hospital, Delhi)

Definium Therapeutics said on Wednesday its LSD-based experimental pill significantly reduced anxiety symptoms in a late-stage study, meeting the trial's main goal and sending the drug developer's shares up more than 20% premarket.
The 214-patient trial tested a single 100-microgram dose of DT120, a fast-dissolving tablet of lysergide, the chemical name for LSD, in adults with generalized anxiety disorder, or GAD.
Patients on the drug had an 11.6-point drop on a standard anxiety rating scale at week 12, compared with a 6.2-point drop for those on a placebo.
The placebo-adjusted difference of 5.4 points was statistically significant and clinically meaningful, the company said.
RBC Capital Markets analyst Brian Abrahams said the data exceeded Wall Street's expectations and the efficacy seen with other therapies for the disease.
The benefit emerged as early as two days after dosing and lasted throughout the 12-week study.
The drug belongs to a class of compounds known as psychedelic medicines.
Regulatory and investor enthusiasm for psychedelic-based therapies has helped Definium shares more than triple so far this year.
In April, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to speed up access to research and treatments based on psychedelic drugs for serious mental health conditions.
GAD is characterised by persistent and excessive worry that can interfere with daily life. It affects about 26 million U.S. adults and is commonly treated with antidepressants, anti-anxiety medicines and psychotherapy.
No new drug has been approved for the condition in nearly two decades, according to Brian Barnett, a Cleveland Clinic psychiatrist who worked on the study.
Unlike most anxiety medicines, which are typically taken regularly, DT120 is designed to be administered as a single dose during a monitored dosing session. It works by acting on brain receptors involved in mood and perception.
Most side effects were mild to moderate and temporary,occurring mainly on the day of dosing, with no increase in suicidal thoughts.
The trial is Definium's second late-stage success for DT120, following a positive readout in a depression study in June.

The Assam Pradesh Congress Committee (APCC) on Wednesday (August 13, 2026) submitted a memorandum to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, urging him to declare the state's recurring flood and river erosion crisis a 'national problem'.
A delegation led by Pranjit Das, Chairman of the APCC Relief & Rehabilitation Department, met Assam Governor Lakshman Prasad Acharya and submitted the memorandum in this regard.
The flood situation in Assam improved on Wednesday (August 13, 2026) as the number of affected people dipped to 87,000 in four districts, but the toll climbed to 103 as two more deaths were reported.
In the memorandum, the Congress said around 40% of Assam's total land area, or 31.05 lakh hectares, is flood-prone, much higher than the national average of 10.2%.
It cited heavy siltation in the Brahmaputra and Barak basins, torrential monsoon rains, shallow riverbeds, embankment breaches and climate change impacts as key factors aggravating the situation.
The crisis has destroyed the livelihoods of farmers, daily wage labourers and tea garden workers, and displaced countless families, it added.
The APCC said the scale of the problem is beyond the capacity of the State government alone and demanded that the Centre recognise it as a "national problem" to ensure a permanent and scientific solution.
The party urged the Centre to set up a high-level task force comprising central and State officials, scientists, technical experts and representatives of affected people to find a solution to the perennial problem.
It also sought adequate central funds for a comprehensive master plan covering river course regulation, embankment strengthening, scientific dredging, real-time flood forecasting, early warning systems and planned rehabilitation of displaced families.
The memorandum further stressed the need for effective coordination among central ministries for integrated management of the Brahmaputra and its tributaries.
"Temporary relief alone cannot provide a lasting solution to this long-standing crisis," it added.

The upcoming action thriller, 7 Dogs, which features Salman Khan and Sanjay Dutt in cameos, will be released in India in Hindi and English on August 21, the makers announced recently. Its trailer was unveiled on Thursday (August 13, 2026).
The Saudi Arabian action film also stars Egyptian superstars Karim Abdel Aziz and Ahmed Ezz along with Monica Bellucci and Giancarlo Esposito.
The action-packed trailer gives a glimpse into the high-octane world of the film which centers around Karim and Ahmed, who form an unlikely buddy-cop partnership to take on an international network of criminals. Salman and Sanjay make goofy appearances in the thrilling trailer, as they partake in the action sequences along with Karim and Ahmed and are seen cracking jokes. Monica makes a brief appearance in the trailer as well, adding on to the mystery around her character as the film promises to take the star-power of them all to create an entertaining spectacle.
Directed by Adil El Arbi and Bilall Fallah (Bad Boys for Life (2020) and Bad Boys: Ride or Die (2024)) and written by Mohamed El-Dabbah from a story by Turki Alalshikh, 7 Dogs features stunts designed by Stephen Dunlevy, whose credits include Mad Max: Fury Road and John Wick.
The ensemble cast also features Tara Emad, Nasser Al-Qasabi and Max Huang, among others, adding on to the diversity of the cross-cultural cinematic collaboration.
7 Dogs is produced by Sela Studios with the support of the General Entertainment Authority (GEA) and Riyadh Season. It was released in the Middle East on May 27 earlier this year following its premiere in Cairo on May 22.

On the last day of the Parliament Monsoon Session on Thursday (August 13, 2026), Leader of the Opposition Mallikarjun Kharge in the Rajya Sabha condemned the ‘shuddhikaran’ (purification) ceremony reportedly held at Haldwani’s Ramlila Ground after he addressed a rally there on Saturday (August 8).
Uttarakhand Congress president Ganesh Godiyal alleged that the Shri Ram Sena, which conducted the ritual, had links to the BJP and the purification was done because Mr. Kharge is a Dalit. He accused the BJP of promoting caste-based divisions and described the incident as deeply objectionable.
“If Kharge ji is insulted, that means everyone is insulted,” said Rajya Sabha Chairman C.P. Radhakrishnan before allowing Mr. Kharge to speak on the incident.
Parliament Monsoon Session Day 19 updates
“I say, with a lot if regret, that I went to deliver a public address at Haldwani. At that time, I did not take any religion’s name, only brought up people’s issues. After my speech, people of the BJP did a “shuddikaran”. Is this the way in democracy? How are you protecting the Constitution?” Mr. Kharge said, amid uproar.
Nadda says enquiry will be initiated
Leader of the House J.P. Nadda slammed the ‘shuddhikaran’ (purification) ceremony, saying that an enquiry will be initiated into the incident and action will be taken against the people involved. Mr. Nadda said, “What Kharge said, it is truly unfortunate. Not just for the Congress, but for all of us.”
Claiming that BJP does not subscribe to such activity, Mr. Nadda said, “Because he said they were BJP people, I want to clarify that the BJP does not subscribe to such activities. But because of the claims, we will investigate. National President Nitin Nabin will take this seriously. We apologise for the hurt it has caused to you.”
“I did not want to make this a political matter. I am in the House for so many years but have never sought sympathy over belonging to the Dalit community,” Mr. Kharge responded. He also demanded a case to be registered under the Untouchability Act, saying, “Register a case against this act of untouchability. That is my demand,” Mr. Kharge said.

The Kerala High Court has claimed to have achieved a significant increase in the number of matters available for hearing and disposal through the recently introduced Auto Cause List System (ACLS) and the campaigns undertaken by the Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) to settle the cases.
The ACLS automatically identifies long-pending cases, prioritises them for listing before the appropriate Benches, and ensures regular and systematic listing of newly instituted cases. The campaign was led by Chief Justice Soumen Sen, according to a communication. Since its introduction on May 19, 2026, a total of 2,02,729 cases were listed before various Benches.
Of the 6,560 cases referred to the Kerala State Mediation and Conciliation Centre of the High Court from January to June 2026, as many as 724 cases were settled at the High Court and 18,110 cases in the district judiciary. The adalats conducted by the High Court Legal Services Committee and the National Lok Adalats organised across the State by the Kerala State Legal Services Authority (KeLSA) have settled 24,682 cases throughout the State. The High Court Legal Services Committee alone settled 70 cases in the High Court through the Adalats. The combined efforts of the agencies have helped the High Court achieve a higher case clearance ratio, according to a communication.
Victim compensation claims
KeLSA also facilitated the release of ₹48.23 crore for pending victim compensation claims across the State.
The scheme provides financial assistance to victims of crime, including women or their dependents, who have suffered loss or injury as a result of the crime and require rehabilitation, the communication said.

The Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Roorkee has launched a four-month postgraduate certificate programme in Building AI-Powered Business Applications, which has been designed by the institute’s iHUB DivyaSampark to equip working professionals who seek to go beyond using artificial intelligence tools and discover building practical AI-powered solutions for business without the need for coding.
The iHUB DivyaSampark, IIT Roorkee, has introduced this programme to guide business professionals on making AI-powered applications without requiring the essential knowledge of coding by offering them AI-powered applications using no-code approaches, AI agents, and intelligent workflow automation.
As per the McKinsey Global Survey: The State of AI in 2025, as much as 88% of organisations have incorporated Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools for their everyday work tasks. Though the dependence on AI continues to be dominant, implementing and scaling AI remains a challenge. The IDC’s Skills, AI and the Enterprise report highlighted that critical AI skills shortages are related to implementation and scaling. Observing the above parity, IIT Roorkee added this programme to its curriculum to assist working professionals to cope with the increasing integration of AI into everyday operations.
Under the iHUB DivyaSampark certificate programme, participants will try their hands on more than 15 AI and automation tools, comprising ChatGPT, Perplexity, NotebookLM, Dify, Flowise, n8n, Make and Airtable. Participants will also learn about Generative AI and Agentic AI, responsible AI, governance, security and deployment readiness. The programme will demonstrate how AI can be applied across fields such as research, reporting, operations, collaboration and decision-making workflows.
The total fee for this programme is Rs 1,09,000, exclusive of GST. Participants who complete the programme will receive an e-Certificate from iHUB DivyaSampark, IIT Roorkee.
All the candidates who have a graduation or diploma degree along with a minimum of three years of work experience can apply for this certificate programme. iHUB DivyaSampark will deliver lectures through live online weekend sessions, with three-hour classes on Saturdays and Sundays. Candidates do not mandatorily require prior coding experience to be eligible for this programme.

The Traitors 2 review: Karan Johar’s show serves both trauma and drama
The Traitors Season 2 review: Dalip Tahil gets evicted, Mallika Sherawat's fancy lifestyle gets judged by other contestants on this game of deception hosted by Karan Johar.
The Traitors 2 review:Karan Johar-hosted The Traitors Season 2 premiered at midnight on Thursday. This season, the show has 21 contestants, and the game of deception began even before the players reached Jaislamer’s Suryagarh Palace. Interestingly, the makers have managed to bring some popular names this season. Popular TV actresses Shweta Tiwari and Krystle D’Souza, chef Ranveer Brar, actresses Mallika Sherawat and Rhea Chakraborty, and internet personalities Munawar Faruqui, Shalini Passi, and Abhishek Malhan are contestants this season.
While host Karan Johar’s fashionable yet savage stance on the show is on point, his one-liners are not quite as impactful. The mix of contestants is quite interesting; however, the strong contenders will only emerge as the season progresses. Like last year, as the contestants started bonding as well as judging each other, Karan Johar also selected the traitors for this season. The contestants arrived in seven cars and were asked to choose one car; the contestants from that car wouldn’t go to the palace. After mutual discussion, Dalip Tahil, Prish, and Ikka decided to go in the other direction.
Krystle D’Souza becomes a traitor; Shweta Tiwari talks about infidelity
After the contestants arrived at the venue, Karan Johar met with everyone personally. When he asked Shweta Tiwari why she wanted to play this game, Shweta said, “I have always followed someone’s direction; here it’s a mind game.” Later, when Karan asked Shweta if she wanted to be a traitor or an innocent, the Kasautii Zindagi Kay actress said, “I am good at lying, which is why I am an actor.” While Karan agreed, he said she might not be great at catching people’s deception. Shweta laughed and said, “It was I who caught my husband cheating.”
At the show’s trailer launch, Shweta had said, “Enough of me being Prerna. Being Prerna, I even got cheated on a lot. Now it’s time to return the betrayal. All I want to tell those who betray is that when a woman stands for herself, even the devil takes notes. So it’s time to take Prerna from the OG Prerna.”
Later, in the ‘Circle of Shaq’ (a table where contestants confront each other and evict one of them), Karan Johar chose Krsytle D’souza, Harma Singha, and Kullu as the three traitors. Later, these three were given the power to recruit the fourth traitor, and they chose Shubhman Gill’s sister, Shahneel, to join them. On the very first day, two contestants were evicted, while Munawar Faruqui’s involvement in the game started bothering other contestants.
Rhea Chakraborty revisits her jail term, Mallika Sherawat flaunts her fancy lifestyle
This season, the actors versus influencers divide seems very evident. Rida Tharana and Abhishek Malhan, in their videos, said that they couldn’t trust the actors because they always put on an act. Abhishek also added that he would like to see how well can he decode personalities of such actors on the show. Mallika Sherawat came in his line of fire right from the first moment. As the arrived to the palace in the same car, Mallika told Abhishek, “I shopped from Paris for this show. I have been building my wardrobe for one and a half months. My fashion game is bang on.”
Later, in his video diary, Abhishek Malhan said that he thought Mallika was too smart to focus only on her fashion game. He said, “I want to see if I can read such actors or not.” In the palace, as Mallika was judged for flaunting her outfit, she told others, “I don’t need validation from anyone; I don’t want to prove to anyone that I have a fabulous life – Paris, LA, Presidents, White House. I don’t need to do drama here.” During her conversation with Karan Johar, when she was asked if she wanted to be a traitor, Mallika refused and said, “Traitors live in the shadows, but I live in the spotlight, and how can the spotlight not always be on the queen? So I want to be an innocent.”
Rhea Chakraborty also appears on the show, and in the first episode, the actress spoke about the Sudhant Singh Rajput death case and her jail term for 27 days in a related drug charge. On her very first appearance in the episode, Rhea said, “I have seen a lot in life, and that will help me in this journey. When a person goes through trauma, there is a gift on the other end, which is to read the world and people around you better. That will help me in this show.”

Later, while talking to Karan Johar, when Rhea was asked if she wanted to be a traitor, the actress refused and explained, “I want to be innocent. This year I have gotten a clean chit, and people have discovered that I was innocent. I have been under suspicion for a while, so I don’t like that anymore.”
After choosing the traitors, all the contestants went to perform a task where they met with Dalip Tahil, Prish, and Ikka. They had to save any two contestants while one would go out. In this task, Dalip Tahil got evicted.
Our Verdict
Given the mix of contestants, this season looks very promising. While Karan Johar tries hard to come across as intimidating, it looks forced. The stylish appearance dominates the attitude. At this point, the show looks a little predictable in terms of who would get evicted first, but how things take a turn, only time will tell. As Karan Johar mentioned at the show’s trailer launch, “This season shocked, surprised, appalled, and even terrified me. I saw the level of betrayal, attack, manipulation, and strategy that I was not expecting. At one point, it stopped becoming a game. Literally every night there was an attack and a stab in the back.”
The Traitors Season 2 streams on Amazon Prime; a new episode drops every Thursday at midnight.

The Bihar cabinet on Wednesday (August 12, 2026) gave its nod to develop 300 ‘stand-alone’ private teacher education institutions (B.Ed.) operating in Bihar into multidisciplinary degree colleges.
The decision will add another 300 additional degree colleges which will offer undergraduate programmes in Arts, Science, Commerce, and other disciplines along with teacher education (B.Ed.) and skill-based courses, Cabinet Secretariat Department’s Secretary Mohammad Sohail said in a post cabinet briefing.
The decision was taken in accordance with the National Education Policy (NEP), 2020, and the guidelines of the National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE), he added.
The new academic programmes will be conducted in accordance with the standards and necessary approvals prescribed by the concerned university, UGC, NCTE, and the State government, Mr. Sohail said.
The initiative will provide students with greater opportunities for higher education within their own district or nearby areas, strengthen access to higher education, and contribute to increasing the state’s Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER), he added.
Extension of Schemes
It also gave the higher education department’s proposal to extend the Bihar Student Credit Card Scheme for another five years from 2026-27 to 2030-31, Mr. Sohail said, adding that ₹950 crore has been approved to be spent in the current financial year 2026-27.
Stating 4.15 lakh students have been benefitted from the SCC scheme, he said this decision will provide students in the State with greater opportunities for higher education, strengthen access to higher education, and promote an increase in the State’s Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER).
A step towards connecting Bihar’s youth with new age employment opportunities, the cabinet also extended the period of ‘Kushal Yuva Programme’ from 2026-27 to 2030-31 under ‘Seven Nischay Part-3’.
It approved ₹430.08 crore for imparting training to youth in future skills such as AI, drones, solar, networking, digital marketing, banking, telecom, foreign languages, and entrepreneurship, the Secretary said and added that it will directly create 6,436 employment opportunities and train 2,57,440 lakh youth annually.
Financial Assistance
In another decision, the cabinet also approved an estimated expenditure of ₹1,000 crore for a period of one year under “Pradhan Mantri Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana”, Mr. Sohail said, adding that the State government would give ₹10,000 per kilowatt subject to a maximum of ₹20,000 through DBT as financial assistance to the residential consumers for installing rooftop solar panels.
The State government’s financial assistance will be given in addition to the central government’s share, he added.
It also decided to set up Compressed Biogas (CBG) plants in four municipal corporations of Gaya Ji, Muzaffarpur, Bhagalpur and Biharsharif (Nalanda) for providing a sustainable solution for waste management by converting organic waste into a valuable renewable energy source, Mr. Sohail said.
The government would give 10 acres of land for a period of 25 years to IOCL, HPCL, BPCL and GAIL for the purpose, he said adding that CBG plants process organic waste and convert it into a valuable energy resource, thereby improving waste management.
Restriction lifted
In yet another decision, the cabinet also lifted the restriction imposed on the purchase, sale, and transfer of land in the notified Greenfield Satellite Cities following the final publication of the Development Plan, Mr. Sohail said.
In addition, the Bihar Urban Development Authority will have the power to lift the restriction on the purchase, sale, and transfer of land after the publication of the draft Development Plan.
The cabinet also approved the Youth, Employment and Skill Development Department’s proposal to amend the admission process for the State’s Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) and to conduct admissions to 50% of the total sanctioned seats in private Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs through the Bihar Combined Entrance Competitive Examination Board (BCECEB), Patna.
A total of 11 decisions were taken at cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary on Wednesday (August 12, 2026).

Kharge raises Uttarakhand post-rally ‘purification’, Rajya Sabha chair seeks probe
Kharge said he is not making it a political issue, but a case under the Untouchability (Offences) Act should be filed and the accused should be arrested
Rajya Sabha chairman CP Radha Krishnan on Thursday instructed the government to conduct a thorough inquiry into the alleged “purification of a site” where Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge addressed a gathering in Uttarakhand and said action must be taken against the guilty.
The instruction came after Kharge spoke about the issue in the Upper House. He said some “BJP [Bharatiya Janata Party] people” carried out the purification at Haldwani’s Ram Lila Maidan, where he addressed the gathering.
The BJP is in power in Uttarakhand, which is due to go to polls next year.
Track Parliament monsoon session LIVE updates
Kharge said he did not take the name of any religion, and only referred to problems being faced by people. “…but some BJP people conducted a havan at the stage and shuddikaran [purification]…is this the way in a democracy… I am the leader of the Opposition [in Rajya Sabha],” he said.
Kharge said he is not making it a political issue, but a case under the Untouchability (Offences) Act should be filed against the accused, and they should be arrested.
Untouchability is outlawed, and practising it in any form is a punishable offence.
Kharge said he has been in this House for years and never said he is a Scheduled Caste, a Dalit, and needs protection. “I am capable of fighting …” he said.

Amid shouting from both sides, Union minister and the House leader JP Nadda said the BJP condemns the incident. “The BJP does not subscribe to such activities. The incident is painful not just for the Congress but for all of us…”
As the Opposition continued to protest, Nadda said an investigation will be conducted and assured the House that action will be taken. “We condemn this, and this is a regrettable issue for all of us,” Nadda said. He objected to Kharge using the term “you people” while referring to the incident.
Krishnan said an insult to Kharge was an insult to everyone. “If untouchability is not a sin, then there is no sin in the world… we all condemn untouchability…all are purified and no need for anyone to purify us again and again…” He then directed the government to investigate and punish the guilty.
Congress Uttarakhand’s unit on Wednesday alleged that people linked to the ruling BJP carried out the purification ritual on the stage after Kharge’s address.

At the pre-release event of the Telugu film Agadha in Hyderabad, Dr Kamakshi Bhaskarla became emotional as she spoke about playing the central character in a film for the first time. It had taken her nine years to reach this point, she said, thanking the audience for their support. Directed by MS Raju, the thriller releases in theatres on August 14.
Settling down for this interview, Kamakshi says she is still a work in progress. “I had to make tough choices in life. There were times when I wanted to give up. But I used the opportunities that came my way to build my career; I had no godfather in the industry.”
Kamakshi made her Telugu cinema debut with Priyuralu and went on to act in several web series and films, including the recent Dacoit. The horror-thriller Maa Oori Polimera proved to be a turning point. She is now working on Polimera 3 and the second season of the web series Dhootha. In her early years, she says, she chose some films for visibility and financial independence, while also gravitating towards characters that represented everyday women.
“In Agadha, my character Mahadevi is central to the film, and it has taken me a while to reach this space,” she says. Kamakshi is aware that her roles in the Polimera franchise, Virupaksha and now Agadha may lead audiences to associate her with thrillers. “Love stories and thrillers remain the most common genres in Telugu cinema where women get to shine. It would be lovely to see well-written comedies that give female characters ample scope.”
Aspiring to write and direct
She dreams of writing and directing a feature film and is pursuing an online screenwriting course. “I worked as an assistant director on Polimera and hope to direct someday. I enjoy work that stimulates me emotionally and intellectually.”
That search for creative and intellectually challenging work led her to theatre before cinema. After returning from China in 2017 with a medical degree, she briefly explored modelling before joining theatre groups Samahaara in Hyderabad and Neeraj Kabi’s group in Mumbai. “Modelling did not interest me. Theatre gave me the creative freedom I was looking for.”
The shift from medicine to theatre and cinema was a conscious attempt to carve out her own path. “I grew up in a middle-class family, in dysfunctional circumstances. I admired the strength of the women in my family but also saw how their voices were suppressed.” She says moving to China for medical studies was partly an attempt to break free and grow independently.
In her early years, she approached production houses and auditioned extensively. “Word got around that there’s a doctor-turned-actor who is good at auditions and is a promising actor,” she recalls with a smile.
She gravitated towards characters representing women often overlooked by mainstream cinema. She played a househelp in Priyuralu and a woman from the fishing community in Polimera. “Such characters are often relegated to supporting parts or not celebrated like the archetypal heroine roles,” she says.
Behavioural psychology
Her understanding of human psychology, she says, helps her inhabit these characters with confidence. “It was one of the subjects in medical school; it taught me to read between the lines and understand a character better.”
While Kamakshi enjoys hearing directors narrate a story, she reads each script several times. “I might have read the script of Polimera over 20 times. I read between the lines to understand what the writer or director intends to convey and whether that intent comes through. If something doesn’t add up, I discuss it with them. Most directors have been welcoming of these conversations.”
Reading has been a source of comfort since childhood. “That was my safe space. I enjoyed having imaginary conversations with the characters in a story.” She is currently reading The Palace of Illusions, a habit that has also sharpened her ability to assess scripts.
Away from film sets, Kamakshi enjoys solo travel and trekking, and hopes to climb Mt Kilimanjaro. “Wherever I travel, I choose homestays so I can be around people and observe them.”
Among women in Telugu cinema, she admires Samantha Ruth Prabhu for shaping her career and building the stardom to headline female-centric films. She also admires Nithya Menen and Nivetha Thomas. “There are a hundred ways to work and survive, but I am consciously choosing films that excite me. I hope my work is emotionally satisfying too.”

BEIJING , Aug. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Recently, iQIYI, China's leading online entertainment platform, has launched Undercurrent Theater , a horizontal-screen short-form suspense brand making a strong debut with its inaugural title "Dead of Winter". The title has gained rapid audience traction and delivered solid commercial returns, signaling strong market appetite for the format. The launch sets a strong foundation for Undercurrent Theater as iQIYI deepens its leadership in premium suspense content.
Since its August 4 premiere, "Dead of Winter" has reached a peak iQIYI content popularity index, a measure of audience engagement on the platform, of 6,638, the highest for an iQIYI revenue-sharing, a model where production partners share earnings with iQIYI based on viewership, short-form drama since 2024. It has also topped multiple industry rankings across leading Chinese entertainment data providers Enlightent, Maoyan and DataWin. Enlightent data shows its daily market share peaked at 60.9%, making it the second horizontal short-form drama this year to surpass 60%, following iQIYI's "The Ferry Man 10th Anniversary", a 10th-anniversary return of the classic IP "The Ferry Man".
Strong viewership has also translated into commercial momentum. Within five days of release, "Dead of Winter" generated over RMB5 million (approximately US$740,000) in revenue-sharing earnings, with iQIYI projecting total revenue-sharing earnings to exceed RMB10 million (approximately US$1,480,000) within nine days of release.
Set in a small northeastern Chinese city in the late 1990s, "Dead of Winter" is a gritty crime suspense drama rooted in social realism. The series follows two former friends – a community police officer and a criminal investigator – who reunite to solve a series of major cases, unraveling an eight-year family tragedy. Its fast-paced storytelling, strong performances, and distinctive wintry setting have driven significant social buzz. More than 20 derivative short videos have each surpassed 100,000 likes, with audience calls for a second season.
The debut validates both the premium content model and the revenue-sharing approach underpinning Undercurrent Theater, with more titles already in the pipeline. "The VI Group of Fatal Case" (the Chinese title translates as Sixth Criminal Investigation Unit), a prequel to the beloved 2001 crime procedural. "The Murder Truth", adapted from a highly rated original work, weaves intricate deduction with interconnected serial crimes for a layered viewing experience. Together, the upcoming slate builds on the momentum of "Dead of Winter" as iQIYI continues to deepen its short-form suspense offering and cement its position as the home of premium Chinese suspense storytelling for global audiences.

The Supreme Court of India on Thursday (August 13, 2026) asked the union government to consider a petition filed by an apex court lawyer flagging the lack of a comprehensive statutory regime on the government’s use of “high-risk” Artificial Intelligence technology in areas affecting public access to food, health benefits, wages, pension, scholarship and grant of welfare subsidies.
A three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant asked the government to consider the detailed petition of advocate N.K. Goswami as a representation for taking comprehensive action.
In his petition, Mr. Goswami questioned whether the government could employ AI, machine learning (ML), automated decision-making systems, risk-scoring mechanisms, biometric surveillance tools, predictive policing technologies and AI-assisted content moderation systems in crucial areas of governance affecting welfare, liberty, privacy, dignity, livelihood and speech, without a “specific statutory framework” or meaningful human oversight.
The lawyer clarified that the constitutional vice pleaded in the petition was not that technology must be prohibited.
“The vice is that technology affecting fundamental rights cannot be permitted to operate outside the discipline of the Constitution. When a citizen’s access to food, health benefits, wages, pension, scholarship, subsidy, liberty, privacy or speech is affected by an opaque automated or semi-automated system, the State must satisfy the minimum constitutional requirements,” Mr. Goswami submitted.
The petition said he was only trying to constitutionalise innovation.
“AI is no longer merely an administrative aid or technological convenience. It has begun to enter the bloodstream of governance. Public-domain official materials, policy and supporting documents show that AI/ML, automated decision-making, fraud-detection, beneficiary-verification, Aadhaar-linked authentication, data-driven de-duplication and similar algorithmic systems are being used in welfare-linked governance, from health-benefit delivery to ration-distribution optimisation to fraud-prevention,” it said.
The Chief Justice said the petition raised technical issues in the policy domain, and the court lacked the necessary technical know-how to address them.
Mr Goswami argued that the court could indeed intervene to fill the legislative gap, given the lack of any statutory mechanism governing the use of AI/ML in public welfare.
The petition had sought that the court direct the Centre to file a “complete affidavit” disclosing all existing and proposed high-risk AI systems used by Union Ministries/agencies in welfare, policing, surveillance and content regulation, together with their legal basis, vendor/agency, purpose, data categories, safeguards, grievance mechanism and audit status.

An attempt made by a railway gatekeeper at Gopurarajapuram near Papanasam in Thanjavur district to save another person from being run over by a train on Wednesday (August 12, 2026) night cost him his life.
Inquiries reveal that the gatekeeper, Rahul Kumar (30) of Keerthai hamlet, Baghpat district, Uttar Pradesh, who was posted for duty at the level crossing (LC) gate at Gopurarajapuram, saw a person heading towards the railway track while the Nagercoil-Tambaram Antyodaya Express was fast approaching the LC at around 11.45 p.m. on August 12.
Immediately, he ran towards the person and attempted to pull him to safety. However, the person was hit by the speeding train, and in the process, the gatekeeper too was killed. The identity of the person whom the railway gatekeeper attempted to save but who was also killed in the accident had yet to be identified, according to official sources.

In 1989 when Collin Timms opened a Mexican restaurant in Bengaluru named after a river in New Mexico, Pecos, it bombed. People were simply not familiar with the cuisine. It is another story that Pecos eventually pivoted to selling beer and became the city’s favourite pub. Today, things are very different when it comes to Mexican food. Carne asadas and birria tacos are fast selling dishes in the city’s new age restaurants, that focus on regional dishes and authenticity. We trace this evolution and explore the new fascination Bengaluru has for the cuisine.
Chef Varun Pereira, the man behind the restaurant Comal, says, “There has been a huge increase in interest for Mexican cuisine. Even the Tex Mex places are now adding Mexican dishes to their menus. I feel it is a very unexplored cuisine. Mexican was never as popular as Italian or Asian. But there is a huge connect between Indian and Mexico.” At Comal you can dine on masa flour tortillas and chilaquiles. The focus is on using techniques, tools (comal means tawa) and ingredients. The tortillas are made with nixtamalization of corn flour and the enchiladas have mole sauce. Their best sellers are jackfruit flautas (rolled-up tacos), horchata, the rice-based drink, and carne asadas (grilled and sliced meat dish).
Varun, with co-founder Pratheek Reddy travelled to Mexico City for a month and ate in Michelin-starred restaurants and street tacos. “I am a big fan of Mexican cuisine, and there was always a gap in the market, and I wanted to bring my love for this food to India and Bengaluru.”
At Comal there are tables facing the open kitchen so guests can chat and give immediate feedback to the chefs. He says the Bengaluru diner is open to new cuisines, compared to other cities. “We get guests who are not familiar with the cuisine and want to be guided through, it is nice to have that option.”
Cantina culture
For restauranteur Rizwan Amlani, opening Mezcalita, a cantina-style establishment was a labour of love. When he was in his 20s, working as a chef in the US, he would go to Mexico often and it almost felt like home. His passion for the country and knowledge of the cuisine is evident as he describes to me the difference between a cantina, a taquería, and a fondita (it is a home-style eatery, if you are curious).
“A cantina is a friendly casual establishment. The bartends will know your name, it is a family affair. It is like an Irani cafe in Mumbai. I go to the same Irani cafe, my great grandfather went to.” Mezcalita has outlets in Mumbai and Bengaluru, and their top sellers are the Baja fish taco, pork carnitas and green enchiladas. The Bengaluru diner, he says, is the most experimental and curious. “My team is challenged every day because people ask a lot of questions. They want to know how it is cooked, what are the spices, why is it so familiar. This is rarer in Mumbai.”
Chocolate in my gravy?
Chinita is a one of the few Mexican restaurants that opened a decade ago. “When we first started, we spent a lot of time on the floor talking to customers, educating them about the cuisine and explaining the various dishes on our menu. Over the last 12 years, we’ve noticed that the cuisine has become more widely accepted and popular, and customers are more knowledgeable about Mexican food now,” says Sameer Mirchandani, the managing partner at the restaurant that has outlets in Koramangala and Indiranagar.
“I remember certain traditional Mexican combinations used to generate a lot of interest, such as chocolate and chilli in our chocolate chilli cake, and the idea of using chocolate in a main course like in our mole.” Their soft tacos, burrito bowls, chocolate chilli cake, and Mexican-style grilled corn have been some of the best-sellers from the start.
Another restaurant in Indiranagar serving regional Mexican food is the newly opened Comedor. With a vegetarian only menu, it has dishes such as chile relleno (stuffed chillies) that hail from the city of Puebla, and Sopa de fideo (a vermicelli soup with Spanish roots). Ingredients such as Mexican pepperleaf, masa flour, cojita cheese and the root vegetable jicama are used in the dishes.
Rizwan feels there are not enough Mexican spaces in India. “Bengaluru diners are experimental, but I feel like every market in India is still not ready to go down that path yet. However, there is scope in the future for regional Mexican food.” He compares it to how Asian food used to be monolith earlier, and now we have specialty spaces. “I would love to do an Oxacan restaurant someday.”

Rohini Rana’s new cookbook Memories on a Platter: My Fusion Cookbook begins with a dedication to the three women who ignited a love of cooking in her – her mother, her sister-in-law and her husband’s nanny — a flame that, decades later, continues to burn.
Born into royalty to Raja Digvijay Pal Singh and Rani Anant Kumari of Awagarh in Uttar Pradesh, Rohini married Gaurav Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana, who went on to become the Chief of Army Staff, Nepal Army, from 2012 to 2015.
“During the eight months between my engagement and marriage, my mother realised that I had not learnt any cooking skills – owing to my years of staying in hostel dorms and only coming home for the holidays. So, my sister-in-law, Rani Saheba Anjali Kumari, was tasked with teaching me how to cook. From making eggs-to-order to sandwiches and cakes as well as Indian dishes, she taught me all, and I absorbed it like a sponge!”, Rohini recalls with a smile. As a newly-married bride in Nepal, it was her husband’s childhood nanny, Chiniya Champa didi, who taught her cooking. “I’ve been a foodie my whole life. I guess that is what led to my interest in cooking because once you’re fond of eating good food, you want to know how to make it,” she says.
It was out of sheer boredom, when her husband was posted somewhere in the hills, and she found herself the sole woman among a battalion of 800 men, that she decided to pen down an introduction to her first book — The Rana Cookbook: Recipes from the Palaces of Nepal. “I realised that my husband’s nanny was getting old and soon, all that knowledge about Nepalese heritage cuisine would be lost,” she says. The Nepal Cookbook: 108 Regional Recipes followed soon after, both books earning recognition for preserving Nepal’s culinary heritage.
Her third book, Memories on a Platter: My Fusion Cookbook, published by Penguin Random House, was launched recently in the presence of Jyotiraditya M Scindia, Union Minister of Communications. The collection draws inspiration from Rohini’s childhood in India, her years within Nepal’s illustrious Rana family after her marriage, and the diverse cuisines she encountered while accompanying her husband on diplomatic and military assignments around the world. “Having exhausted my Nepali repertoire, I was thinking about what to do next. I think the more you grow older, the more you drift back to your childhood memories. So, I have a lot of Indian recipes in this book, but since it is fusion, there is Nepali cuisine as well as cuisines from places such as Italy, Japan, China, Kenya, Lebanon, Cambodia, the United Kingdom, and Malaysia among many others,” she shares.
Divided into sections such as global bites, centrestage, vibrant crunchy bowls, sweet traditions and liquid delights, the book blends anecdotes from her life with inventive cross-cultural dishes. A great love for all things chaat (she is from UP, after all!) led to a recipe with golgappas, but since this is also fusion, she suggests fillings such as scrambled eggs and salmon, or corn and edamame. Elsewhere, mini makki ki rotis meet melted brie, and buckwheat crepes take on ham and cheese.
“Most of these dishes came out of experiments, and I have, hopefully, taken them to a different level. In a way, this book is my memoir told through food,” she smiles, revealing that she does have an idea for her next cookbook — inspired by India, again — but for now, she is simply enjoying sharing these delicious chapters of her life. As she writes in the introduction — “This book is not in the pursuit of perfection but in the pursuit of joy, the pleasure I gain from being creative and feeding people, which to me is a language of love…”

The Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) government in Kerala on Thursday (August 13, 2026) edged closer to ordering a multi-angled investigation into the previous Left Democratic Front (LDF) government’s “bungled attempt” to bring the 2021 FIFA World Cup-winning Argentina team and its iconic captain, Lionel Messi, for a friendly match at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in Kochi in 2025.
Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan told a press conference that the State Sports Department’s preliminary inquiry into the alleged fiasco, which left football fans profoundly disappointed, revealed “very serious allegations” warranting further investigation by multiple departments and agencies.
(The charges in the report, vetted by Sports Department Special Secretary N. Prasanth, reportedly included massive service tax fraud on foreign remittances, contraventions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), abuse of power resulting in loss to the public exchequer, and “shady financial transactions” involving offshore entities, among other charges.)
Mr Satheesan said the previous government “cannot not shrug off responsibility” centred around the controversy by airing “contradictory statements”.
He said several questions remain unanswered. “What was the procedure followed by the previous government to permit the private sponsor (a television news broadcasting company) to transact with the Argentine Football Association (AFA) on behalf of the State without inviting an expression of intent, a legal pre-requisite before entering into a final binding contract or agreement? Did the government examine the source of the private sponsor’s funding? Did it conduct a market price determination before contemplating a binding legal contract or agreement with the private sponsor?”, Mr Satheesan asked.
The Chief Minister said the Finance Department, which he heads, has opened an investigation into suspected GST levy evasion on foreign remittances, amounting to a projected ₹156 crore, purportedly made by the sponsor to the Argentine Football Association to secure Messi and his team’s presence in Kochi.
“The previous LDF government had flagged the suspected loss to the State exchequer and issued a notice to the sponsor. Inexplicably, the tax enforcement procedure froze overnight”, he said.
Mr Satheesan said a myriad of other “intriguing questions” also begged answers. “What was the State’s role in the LDF government-backed attempt to bring the Argentine team to Kerala? Did the government protect the State’s interests in the process? Did the sponsor seek to exploit the State and use the heft of the government for pursuing personal pecuniary interests?”, he asked.
Mr Satheesan said the government would decide the impending investigation’s “terms of reference”. He said the State would take a call on whether it was required to enlist the services of Central agencies (the Enforcement Directorate or the Central Bureau of Investigation) to probe possible violations of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act and the Prevention of Money Laundering (PMLA) Act.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her role later this month, depriving U.S. President Donald Trump of his chief spokesperson less than three months before the November midterm elections. Ms. Leavitt has served as the press secretary since Mr. Trump returned to office in 2025.
Karoline Leavitt to step down
Mr. Trump announced the move on Wednesday (August 12, 2026) in a post on social media. He said Ms. Leavitt was stepping down to spend more time with her family and would “now be one of my top outside advisors”. She recently gave birth to her second child.
In a separate post, Ms. Leavitt said she was “incredibly grateful” for the opportunity to serve, but added that the position had placed significant demands on her family. She said Mr. Trump had asked her to continue as a “top advisor to him on the outside”.
“The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy and attention required of the White House Press Secretary,” she wrote.
Mr. Trump said Ms. Leavitt “will be departing her role at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family, a decision I totally understand and respect! Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party, as we work to defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections.”
The President did not immediately name a successor, and the White House did not respond to questions about who would replace her.
Trump’s ‘trusted aide’
Mr. Trump, then President-elect, announced on November 15, 2024, that Ms. Leavitt would serve as White House press secretary.
Ms. Leavitt succeeded Karine Jean-Pierre on January 20, 2025, when Mr. Trump was sworn in as the 47th President of the United States. She had previously served as the Trump campaign’s national press secretary and worked in the first Trump administration as the assistant press secretary. While announcing her appointment, the President had said that she was smart, tough, and a highly effective communicator
Ms. Leavitt has been among the most prominent advocates of Mr. Trump’s “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) campaign. Mr. Trump described her as “one of my most trusted aides”.
Youngest White House press secretary
Ms. Leavitt, 28, became the youngest person to serve as White House press secretary when she assumed office last year. She previously worked as a junior spokesperson during Mr. Trump’s first term and later became a leading spokeswoman for his 2024 presidential campaign after an unsuccessful congressional bid in New Hampshire in 2022.
She recently returned to work following maternity leave after the birth of her second child, a daughter, in May. She also has a two-year-old son.
During Ms. Leavitt’s maternity leave in May, the White House held fewer press briefings and did not appoint an interim spokesperson. Instead, senior officials, including Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, conducted media briefings.
Combative approach towards media
During her tenure at the White House, Ms. Leavitt became known for her combative exchanges with the media and her staunch defence of the President.
During Mr. Trump’s first term, Ms. Leavitt served as a press aide in the White House press office before becoming the communications director to New York Republican Representative Elise Stefanik.
In his second term, with Ms. Leavitt as a key public advocate, the White House adopted an even more confrontational media strategy than during his first administration. While Mr. Trump frequently engaged directly with reporters at White House events and during official travel, Ms. Leavitt often appeared on Fox News and other conservative outlets to promote the administration’s agenda and criticise Democrats and mainstream media organisations.
Ms. Leavitt’s departure comes at a challenging time for the U.S. President, who is facing difficulties in finding a path forward on the conflict involving Iran, while also confronting concerns over the economy. These issues have weighed on the President’s approval ratings and raised concerns among Republicans about retaining control of Congress in the midterm elections.

The YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) has urged the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), Andhra Pradesh, and the Election Commission of India (ECI) to make the verification process for electors whose records have been classified as unmapped or mismatched more voter-friendly.
In a representation to the CEO on Wednesday (August 12, 2026), YSRCP State general secretary and MLC Lella Appi Reddy sought uniform instructions across the State on three issues: allowing parents or blood relatives to submit documents on behalf of electors, making the verification venue mandatory in every notice, and providing assistance through Booth Level Officers (BLOs). The party released the letter to the media on Thursday.
Mr. Appi Reddy said in the representation that many affected electors could be students, employees, migrant workers or persons temporarily residing away from their native places, and might not be able to appear personally on the date specified in the notice. He requested that parents or blood relatives be permitted to submit the required documents on behalf of such electors, along with proof of relationship and proper authorisation. This, he said, would help ensure that genuine voters were not excluded merely because they could not be physically present.
Mr. Appi Reddy also said that in some notices, the place of verification had reportedly been left blank. A voter could not reasonably be expected to comply with a notice without knowing where to appear, he said.
He urged the authorities to ensure that every notice clearly mentioned the exact venue, date, time and details of the officer concerned before it was served on the elector.
He also called for greater involvement of BLOs in the verification process. Instead of requiring every elector to approach a higher-level electoral officer personally, the BLO concerned should be involved in receiving documents and conducting preliminary or field-level verification, he suggested.
The final statutory decision could continue to rest with the competent Electoral Registration Officer or Assistant Electoral Registration Officer, while BLO-level facilitation would enable voters to resolve discrepancies locally and quickly, he said.
Mr. Appi Reddy appealed to the Election Commission to issue uniform State-wide instructions on the three issues so that no genuine elector was excluded merely because of procedural difficulties, temporary absence from the constituency or lack of clarity in the verification notice.

The Lok Sabha recently passed an amendment to a law to make it legal to levy surcharges or fees on any UPI and RuPay debit card transactions. The government, meanwhile, announced that it proposes to do so only for purchases of ₹2,000 and more from businesses with a threshold of turnover. But with the legal bar removed, government decisions can change any time.
The stated logic, as the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra recently put it, is that “somebody has to pay” for UPI. The Indian government is said to have subsidised UPI by about ₹2,000 crore in the past one year.
Let us first examine the stated reason, and then come to what most knowledgeable people think is the real reason.
Digital payments such as UPI and debit cards replace the centuries-old payment system of bank notes and coins. The latter can be called physical currency as against the new digital currency. Who paid for the bank notes payment system? The RBI printed notes and minted coins and gave them to the banks for no charges. One can walk into a bank and demand currency notes for all the deposits one held, and they would have to be made available free of charge, even in the precise denominations asked for, subject to availability (though the printing and logistic costs of small notes for the same amount is much more than of big notes).
So, if the government — through the RBI — funded the earlier/ traditional payments system, or more widely, the cost of the “operating medium” of economic exchanges, what prevents it from doing it now as well. What has changed? In fact, a digital “payments system” is far less costly, and much more efficient, than a physical currency-based one.
What is a digital payment system? A user is at a shop and wants to make a purchase. She gives a secure message to her bank to withdraw and spend her own money. Instead of the bank handing them the needed cash, and user giving it to the merchant, and the merchant then depositing it in his bank — a tedious, and quite costly process — a set of instant secure messages just ensures that the user’s account is debited and the merchant’s, perhaps in another bank, credited the same amount. Why should this relatively trivial and inexpensive process — replacing a much more cumbersome and costlier one — be required to separately be paid for, when cash movement itself was not paid for?
If the government spent ₹2,000 crore on UPI last year, it also saved nearly ₹1,500 crore over the same time in reduced expenditure on printing currency notes. This saving is going to go up fast, as digital means replace currency, while UPI operating costs could remain similar, or actually come down as technology advances. If digital systems incur costs on security, physical cash systems also require them, even if of a different kind.
Public goods are generally free
But why should the government make such expenditures at all without recouping them, if possible? There is a very sound economic logic for it. Less or near-nil friction in the payments system, through zero costing of transactions, considerably increases economic flows. The overall economy benefits multiple times more than any possible collection of transaction surcharges. This is the typical public goods logic. This is why governments erect lighthouses on the shores and develop parks in cities. Charging users for such services tend to reduce or distort their use and benefits to such an extent that it is judged unfavourably.
First-time visitors to some European cities are pleasantly surprised when their hotel gives them a transport pass for their entire stay, which is provided free by the city. Such a free pass greatly increases the mobility of the tourists through the city, rather than them scouring for change for every small ride. Tourists moving around spend more money, and do it across the city. The overall economy of the city benefits a lot. Even the government is likely to get back more in sales taxes from such extra spending than what they lost in providing free transport passes.
Similarly, the way increased mobility can increase economic activity — which is why many countries have traditionally subsidised motor fuel — reduced friction in economic transactions does it even more. That is why bank notes were never charged for their production and logistic costs. There is no reason that governments and central banks should charge for the less costly and much more efficient (economic activity expanding) digital payment system. As said, that is just sound economic logic.
If banknote payments require no surcharges or fees, why should digital payments incur them, in a digital world? After all, digital payments means less work and less costs of all kinds for almost everyone involved. When the public goods argument works for physical currency, why should it fail for digital currency?
The real reason
Let us now move to the real reasons for what is happening. Many countries such as Brazil, Indonesia, Vietnam, Turkey, and so on, now have a UPI-like system. Both India and Brazil have repeatedly been named in U.S. official documents regarding their digital payment systems being “unfair trade practices”. In July 2026, the U.S. government imposed a 25% tariff on a range of imports from Brazil, explicitly citing Brazil’s free, state-run instant payment system, Pix, as an unfair trade barrier that disadvantages American financial companies such as Visa and Mastercard.
The India-U.S. trade deal is nearly ready, though its details remain secret. India is currently checking the boxes on U.S. demands. It can be said with almost complete certainty that India has bent where Brazil stood firm. This is why it amended the law which disallowed surcharges on UPI. So that Visa and MasterCard do not suffer. One already sees at retail stores and petrol pumps, merchants making excuses that their credit card machine is not working, and preferring UPI payments, which saves them a considerable surcharge. U.S. President Donald Trump could not let top U.S. financial corporations lose major markets.
When U.S. credit companies emerged, it was a digital innovation over a mainstream physical currency system. Making instant secure communication for payments was quite expensive. Today, it is a rather trivial technology, and the system is much cheaper than physical currency. Also, digital is mainstream today. Some banks worldwide charge for physical interactions, while providing the digital ones free. India suddenly now bringing in fees for digital payments is going against both the economic and technological logic.
Let UPI remain a public good
One thing the Indian government has boasted about the most in the last many years, nationally and internationally, is India’s UPI. It is shocking that under U.S.’s pressure India is willing to change the basic logic and architecture of its most vaunted achievement. Just so that the business model of Visa and Mastercard is not affected. This does not speak well about Indian sovereignty. If Brazil could stand firm, why cannot India?
By banning surcharges or fees on UPI, India will continue to reap the immense gains in terms of economic ease, efficiency and expansion that come from it. UPI is today also a matter of inclusion and social justice. We need not import the U.S. model which wants to see everything, even payment systems, as a market good. UPI should stay a public good, and free.
India should promote a competitive field of payment players, preferably domestic, and leverage a public and free switch of UPI. That way, VIsa and Mastercard, and other foreign companies, may not rule over one of the biggest assets of Indian payments data.
Parminder Jeet Singh is a Delhi-based digital society researcher and activist
